tldr: By post-training the large-scale Cosmos 3 foundation model with a shared causal learning and distillation recipe, the authors build a real-time, streaming neural world simulator for robot manipulation, controllable video transfer, and autonomous driving.
hero_caption: Transitioning from the Cosmos 3 foundation model to interactive world simulators. Using a shared causal learning and distillation recipe, three specialized models are derived: robot manipulation (Sim-Bimanual), physics-driven video transfer (Sim-Transfer), and autonomous driving (Sim-Auto).
overview:
In Physical AI systems such as robots and autonomous vehicles, perception, prediction, and action are tightly coupled because an agent's own actions alter future observations. Training and evaluating these agents solely in the real world is dangerous and expensive, making simulation that combines physical laws with visual diversity indispensable. However, existing video generation models predominantly rely on bidirectional attention across an entire video clip. As a result, they cannot serve as interactive world simulators that respond in real time to sequentially arriving actions or physical states.

To address this challenge, the authors propose a shared post-training framework built on the omnimodal world foundation model Cosmos 3, simultaneously achieving causal (non-anticipating) generation and real-time execution. They establish a four-stage recipe: long-context adaptation, causal Teacher Forcing (TF) training with temporal-causal attention, few-step consistency distillation (TF-dCM), and Self Forcing (SF-DMD), which feeds back generated history to eliminate exposure bias over long rollouts.

They demonstrate this unified framework across three domains: camera navigation and bimanual robot manipulation (Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual), monocular video transfer conditioned on external simulator states (Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Transfer), and autonomous driving with synchronized multi-view cameras and LiDAR (Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto). The resulting models retain strong physical consistency and image quality with just 4 diffusion steps, achieving real-time streaming generation at over 48 FPS on a single GB300 GPU.
contributions: Establishing a shared four-stage post-training recipe (bidirectional adaptation, causal TF, TF-dCM distillation, and SF-DMD) that turns the Cosmos 3 video foundation model into an interactive streaming generation model.

Building Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual, a unified model predicting future video for both camera navigation and bimanual robot manipulation from action sequences, significantly outperforming existing baselines in control fidelity and visual quality.
Realizing Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Transfer, which generates photorealistic RGB video in real time from spatial control signals (depth, segmentation, edges, etc.) provided by an external physics simulator.
Systematizing real-time inference optimizations, including synchronized streaming generation of multi-view video and LiDAR, CUDA Graph capture, KV cache management, and asynchronous decoding.

sections.heading: Toward Interactive World Simulators for Physical AI
sections.summary: Real-world robotics experiments are costly and hazardous, so policy learning and evaluation require high-quality simulation. This paper proposes a shared framework based on Cosmos 3 that streams visual observations in real time in response to incoming actions and control signals.
sections.details:
In Physical AI, agents operate in a closed loop where their own actions induce future observations. However, validating everything in the physical world is brittle and risky. Conventional physics simulators offer accurate dynamics but lack visual diversity such as realistic textures and lighting. Conversely, recent video generative models produce photorealistic footage, but they batch-generate entire clips from predefined prompts, lacking any interactivity.

Building an interactive neural world simulator requires satisfying three core criteria simultaneously: control fidelity, persistence of generated state changes (temporal consistency), and responsiveness on a real-time scale. To achieve this, the authors introduce a shared recipe starting from the Cosmos 3 foundation model, combining causal predictive learning, distillation, and streaming inference.

This paper validates the approach across three Physical AI domains: robot manipulation and camera navigation (Sim-Bimanual), monocular video transfer based on physics simulator states (Sim-Transfer), and multi-view autonomous driving simulation (Sim-Auto), proving that a single underlying design philosophy generalizes across diverse Physical AI workloads.

sections.heading: Designing Temporal-Causal Attention and Multimodal Token Layout
sections.summary: Inheriting the Mixture-of-Transformers architecture of Cosmos 3, the framework introduces temporal-causal attention that forbids referencing future video chunks. Actions and spatial control signals are integrated as clean condition tokens alongside noisy visual target tokens.
sections.details:
### 2.1 Cosmos 3 Backbone
The underlying Cosmos 3 adopts a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture consisting of a "Reasoner" tower dedicated to next-token prediction and a "Generator" tower handling diffusion denoising. Visual features are compressed temporally by a factor of 4 via a causal video VAE, mapping $1+4n$ RGB input frames into $1+n$ latent timesteps. Positional encodings rely on 3D Multimodal RoPE (MRoPE), which treats time, height, and width independently, and a large temporal offset (15,000) separates text from diffusion sequences to prevent cross-modal interference.

### 2.2 Multimodal Token Arrangement
To enable streaming generation, the target output is partitioned into temporal chunks across consecutive latent steps. Chunk $j$ comprises $N_j \ge 1$ latent steps (corresponding to $4N_j$ RGB frames) and is concatenated with its corresponding control signal group $\mathcal{U}_j$ to form a generation unit $\mathcal{G}_j^\tau = [\mathcal{U}_j, \tilde{\mathcal{V}}_j^\tau]$. Crucially, the control tokens $\mathcal{U}_j$ remain uncorrupted (clean) throughout diffusion and are excluded from the loss calculation. Past chunks are preserved as a key-value cache $\mathcal{H}_j^{\text{KV}}$, referenced without recomputation.

### 2.3 Temporal-causal Attention
While the original Cosmos 3 performs bidirectional attention over the entire video clip, this framework replaces it with block-causal (chunk-causal) attention. Queries in the current chunk can attend to all tokens within the same chunk and the clean history $\mathcal{H}_j$ from past chunks, but references to future chunks are strictly masked. This setup prevents the model from peeking ahead and enables autoregressive generation driven by sequentially arriving actions.

captions.P8: Token arrangement for autoregressive video generation with streaming control. Past history $\mathcal{H}_j$ is retained as a KV cache, and in the current chunk $\mathcal{G}_j^\tau$, only the visual tokens $\tilde{\mathcal{V}}_j^\tau$ are iteratively denoised under clean control inputs $\mathcal{U}_j$.

sections.heading: From Causality to Self Forcing: A 4-Stage Post-Training Pipeline
sections.summary: Switching a bidirectional video model to streaming generation all at once degrades quality, so the authors adopt a four-stage process: bidirectional adaptation (Stage 0), causal Teacher Forcing (Stage 1), few-step consistency distillation (Stage 2), and Self Forcing on generated rollouts (Stage 3).
sections.details:
### 3.1 Bidirectional Adaptation (Stage 0)
Before applying causal masks, the model is first adapted to target domain data (action-to-video or control-signal-to-video) under full bidirectional attention across all timesteps. Training with a Rectified Flow objective establishes robust control-to-visual correspondences over long contexts. This model is later frozen and reused as an authoritative reference teacher in Stage 3 distillation.

### 3.2 Causal Training with Teacher Forcing (Stage 1)
Next, temporal-causal masking is introduced to train the model to denoise the current chunk conditioned on clean ground-truth reference history $\mathcal{H}_j$ via Teacher Forcing (TF). To optimize training throughput, a two-pass replay scheme is used: one pass extracts the KV cache from clean history, while a second pass evaluates noisy targets in parallel.

### 3.3 Causal Consistency Distillation With Teacher Forcing (Stage 2)
Because standard diffusion models require dozens of denoising steps, real-time interaction is impossible without acceleration. The authors distill the model using discrete-time consistency distillation (TF-dCM), training a student model to predict the same clean endpoint from different noise levels along the trajectory, reducing generation to about 4 steps. Clean history is still supplied via Teacher Forcing at this stage.

### 3.4 Distribution Matching Distillation with Self Forcing (Stage 3)
When models up to Stage 2 are rolled out autoregressively during inference, accumulated prediction errors quickly lead to visual collapse—a phenomenon known as exposure bias. Self Forcing (SF-DMD) resolves this. The student model takes its own previously generated rollouts as visual history, while the entire generated sequence is evaluated by the frozen Stage 0 bidirectional teacher and a trainable Auxiliary Score Model using a distribution matching loss. This drastically boosts long-horizon consistency and realism while preserving 4-step generation speeds.

sections.heading: Streaming Inference and System Optimizations for Real-Time Interaction
sections.summary: Beyond reducing model steps, the entire system must minimize latency from control input to display. Using bounded KV caching with attention sinks, static compilation with CUDA Graphs, and decoupled asynchronous decoding, the system achieves faster-than-real-time generation.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Streaming State and Memory
The inference loop persistently reuses language representations, the clean generated KV cache, and causal decoder states across chunks. However, retaining all historical tokens as generation progresses would cause memory and attention compute to explode. To keep computation bounded, the authors adopt a bounded KV cache that pairs an "attention sink" region holding initial frames with a rolling window for the most recent frames.

### 4.2 Runtime Optimization
To push control-to-observation latency ($T_{\text{control}\to\text{obs}}$) and generation throughput (FPS and real-time factor RTF) to their limits, several system-level optimizations are introduced:

- Static Compilation and CUDA Graphs: Fixing the KV cache size freezes tensor shapes, enabling static compilation and CUDA Graph capture/replay to eliminate kernel launch overheads.
- Maskless Attention: Instead of materializing large pairwise masks, attention is computed separately over permitted token groups and merged using Log-Sum-Exp statistics, reducing memory traffic.
- Context and Camera Parallelism: For multi-GPU deployment, Ulysses-style context parallelism and pipelining across multiple camera encoders and decoders are implemented.
- Asynchronous Decoding: As soon as a chunk's latent variables are generated, they are transferred to a causal decoder (TAEHV Super or Wan 2.2 VAE) on a separate GPU. The generation GPU proceeds immediately to KV cache updates for the next chunk, completely overlapping decoding with generation.

sections.heading: Unifying Manipulation and Camera Navigation: Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual
sections.summary: This example integrates camera navigation and robot manipulation within a unified 59-dimensional action space. A 4-step SF-DMD student model surpasses dedicated baselines in visual quality and control fidelity during long-horizon tracking and grasping.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Architecture & 5.2 Data Preparation
The authors define a unified 59-dimensional action vector combining ego-camera pose (9D), right wrist/fingertip/gripper poses (24D), and left wrist/fingertip/gripper poses (24D). Missing components are handled via validity masks, allowing a single model to seamlessly cover drone navigation, human hands, and dual-arm robot manipulation. The training mixture blends drone camera footage, AgiBot and YAM robot teleoperation, and egocentric human demonstrations (Mecka) in a 2:2:1 ratio. To prevent text prompts from spoiling future action outcomes, captions are rewritten to describe only the initial scene state.

### 5.3 Post-training & 5.4 Inference Optimization
Causal training uses chunks of 2 latent steps (8 RGB frames), yielding a final 4-step SF-DMD model. With inference optimizations on a single GB300 GPU and the lightweight TAEHV Super decoder, the pipeline clocks a median of 166 ms/chunk (48.1 FPS)—well ahead of a 30 FPS playback rate with a comfortable real-time margin (RTF < 1). Profiling reveals that denoising takes ~89 ms while updating the clean KV cache takes ~69 ms, highlighting that cache update efficiency becomes critical once diffusion is distilled.

### 5.5 Results
In camera navigation benchmarks on PAI-Bench-G and Sana-WM-Bench, Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual outperforms dedicated models like LingBot-World 2.0 and Sana-WM by margins of 8.5 to 11+ visual quality points. On real-robot AgiBot evaluations (World and GEAR splits), it outperforms DreamDojo 14B by ~2 dB in PSNR and achieves lower LPIPS. Ablations show that PSNR, which dropped to 11.85 dB under 4-step TF-dCM, recovers to 13.48 dB with SF-DMD—matching the 13.45 dB fidelity of the bidirectional teacher.

sections.heading: Rendering Photorealistic RGB in Real Time from Simulator Geometry
sections.summary: Sim-Transfer converts spatial control signals (depth, segmentation, edges, blur) derived from external physics simulators (such as Isaac Lab) into photorealistic RGB video with realistic textures and lighting, generating frame-by-frame on a 1-latent-step granularity.
sections.details:
### 6.1 Architecture & 6.2 Data Preparation
Standard graphics outputs from physics simulators often lack visual realism, complicating Sim-to-Real transfer for reinforcement learning policies. Sim-Transfer accepts simulator-derived depth and segmentation maps to render photorealistic video matching user-prompted materials and backgrounds. To minimize response latency, the model operates at the finest temporal granularity of 1 latent step (4 RGB frames) per chunk. Training pairs were extracted from roughly 2 million video clips with temporal captions generated by Qwen3-VL-8B.

### 6.3 Post-training
Training adheres to the four-stage recipe. Attention masks are strictly structured so that control tokens $\mathcal{U}_i$ can be attended up to the current chunk, while noisy RGB queries cannot directly access clean RGB targets in the current chunk. To combat exposure bias during inference, Stage 3 SF-DMD unrolls generation over the model's own past RGB predictions alongside newly streamed simulator controls, guided by the bidirectional teacher and the Auxiliary Score Model. This ensures temporally stable texture rendering that faithfully tracks the simulator's underlying physics.

takeaways: Turning video generation models into world models for robotics requires not just causal masking, but Self Forcing (SF-DMD) on self-generated rollouts to prevent exposure bias.

Once diffusion steps are distilled down (from 35 steps to 4 steps), KV cache updates and decoding become primary bottlenecks, making system-level co-design like asynchronous decoding and bounded caches essential.

Seemingly disparate tasks—such as camera navigation, dual-arm manipulation, and simulator video transfer—can be unified within a single foundation model architecture using clean control tokens paired with noisy visual tokens.
limitations: Current benchmark evaluations focus largely on open-loop prediction over recorded actions or synthetic trajectories; closed-loop reinforcement learning evaluation where policies act directly on generated video requires dedicated validation.

The chunk size (e.g., 2 latent steps = 8 frames) sets the discrete granularity for incoming control signals, meaning faster feedback control operating at millisecond scales demands even lower latency.
Occasional failures in contact mechanics and fine-grained physical interactions still occur, indicating that pure neural generation cannot yet fully replace physics simulation engines.
